items.title: Section: Five Kinds of Abiding Begin — From a Single Fleeting Moment to an Entire Great Eon

items.zh: 一老為緣，能成如上所說一切種老，所謂諸行剎那剎那轉異性老。復次，住差別當知亦有多種，謂剎那住、相續住、緣相續住、不散亂住、立軌範住。若已生諸行生時暫停，名剎那住。若諸眾生，於彼彼處彼彼自體，由彼彼食為依止故，乃至壽住；外器世間大劫量住；名
items.en:
Third, distinctions in abiding; first, stating and listing. Furthermore, the distinctions in abiding should be known to be of many kinds as well: momentary abiding, continuity abiding, abiding through continuity of conditions, undistracted abiding, and abiding by established norm.
Second, explaining each; first, momentary abiding. When an already-arisen conditioned phenomenon momentarily continues at the time of its arising, this is called momentary abiding.
Second, continuity abiding. Sentient beings, relying on this or that kind of nourishment in whatever place and embodiment they occupy, continue on until their lifespan is exhausted; the external physical world abides for the span of a great eon — this is called continuity abiding.

items.title: Section: The Remaining Three Kinds of Abiding — Conditioned Persistence, Undistracted Concentration, and the Rule of Custom

items.zh: 相續住。若樂受、苦受、不苦不樂受，若善、不善、無記法等，乃至各別緣現在前，爾所時住，是名緣相續住。若諸定心由三摩地正起現前，名不散亂住。若於彼彼異方、異域、國城、村邏、王都、王宮，若執理家、商估、邑義諸大眾中，古昔軌範建立隨轉，如是名為立軌範住。
items.en:
Third, abiding through continuity of conditions. Pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling, wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral phenomena, and so on, each abide for however long their own distinct condition remains present before the mind — this is called abiding through continuity of conditions.
Fourth, undistracted abiding. When a mind in meditative concentration is sustained by genuine samādhi actually present and functioning, this is called undistracted abiding.
Fifth, abiding by established norm. In various regions, territories, countries, cities, villages, royal capitals, and royal courts, among judges, merchants, and lay assemblies alike, long-established customs and regulations are followed accordingly — this is called abiding by established norm.

items.title: Section: Six Kinds of Impermanence — From What Ceases as Soon as It Arises to the Very Instant Now Passing

items.zh: 復次，無常差別當知亦有多種，謂壞滅無常、生起無常、變易無常、散壞無常、當有無常、現墮無常。若一切行生已尋滅，名壞滅無常。若一切行本無今有，名生起無常。若可愛諸行異相行起，名變易無常。若不變壞可愛眾具及增上位離散退失，名散壞無常。即四無常，在未來時，名當有無常。即現在世正現前時，名現墮無常。
items.en:
Fourth, distinctions in impermanence; first, distinguishing its characteristics; first, stating and listing. Furthermore, the distinctions in impermanence should be known to be of many kinds as well: impermanence of destruction, impermanence of arising, impermanence of change, impermanence of dispersal, impermanence yet to come, and impermanence presently falling away.
Second, explaining each; first, impermanence of destruction. When all conditioned phenomena, having arisen, soon cease, this is called impermanence of destruction. Second, impermanence of arising. When all conditioned phenomena, originally absent, now come to exist, this is called impermanence of arising. Third, impermanence of change. When desirable conditioned phenomena give rise to an altered, different form, this is called impermanence of change.
Fourth, impermanence of dispersal. When desirable possessions, unchanged in themselves, along with a flourishing position, become scattered or decline, this is called impermanence of dispersal. Fifth, impermanence yet to come. These same four kinds of impermanence, considered as certain to occur in the future, are called impermanence yet to come. Sixth, impermanence presently falling away. The present moment, precisely as it manifests, is called impermanence presently falling away.

items.title: Section: Three Ways of Facing Impermanence — the Grieving Layperson, the Ascetic Who Suppresses, and the Disciple Who Is Finally Free

items.zh: 若受用欲塵多放逸者，但能思惟變易無常、散壞無常、現墮無常，廣起悲歎愁憒憂悴，然於諸行不能厭離。若諸外道，即於如是諸無常性多起思惟，少能方便厭患、離欲，但於諸行一分厭離，不能究竟。若聖弟子圓滿思惟諸無常性，於一切行究竟厭患乃至解脫。
items.en:
Second, a careful analysis; first, householders. Those who indulge heedlessly in sensory pleasure can only contemplate impermanence of change, impermanence of dispersal, and impermanence presently falling away, giving rise to great sorrow, lamentation, grief, confusion, and despair — yet they are unable to develop revulsion towards conditioned existence.
Second, non-Buddhist ascetics. Non-Buddhist ascetics reflect extensively on these very natures of impermanence, and are able to develop some degree of revulsion and freedom from desire, yet this revulsion touches only a portion of conditioned existence, never reaching completion.
Third, noble disciples. Noble disciples fully contemplate every nature of impermanence, and thereby achieve complete revulsion towards all conditioned existence, progressing all the way to liberation.

items.title: Section: "Attainment" Is No Real Thing Either — Refuting the Sarvāstivādin's Substantially Real "Get"

items.zh: 復次，云何得獲成就？謂若略說，生緣攝受增盛之因，說名為得。由此道理，當知得是假有。若言得是實有，此為是諸行生因？為是諸法不離散因？若是諸行生因者，若從先來未得此法，此既無有，生因之得應常不生。由此亦應畢竟不得。若是諸法不離散因者，一切善、不善、無記法，得既俱有，彼雖相違應頓現行。是故二種俱不應理。
items.en:
Second, attainment, acquisition, and accomplishment; first, explaining the distinctions; first, attainment and acquisition; first, the question posed. Furthermore, what are attainment and acquisition?
Second, the explanation; first, briefly in two ways; first, according to a flourishing cause; first, revealing one's own position. In brief, when a supporting condition has taken hold of a phenomenon and brought it to a flourishing, strengthened cause, this is provisionally called attainment. By this reasoning, one should know that attainment has no substantial reality.
Second, refuting the other position; first, the question raised. If attainment is claimed to be substantially real, is it the generating cause of conditioned phenomena, or the cause preventing phenomena from being lost?
Second, the challenge; first, distinguishing; first, the challenge regarding the generating cause of conditioned phenomena. If it is the generating cause, then since one has never, from the beginning, attained this phenomenon's arising, and this attainment does not yet exist, the attainment that generates it should never arise — and by this same reasoning, it should never ultimately be attained at all.
Second, the challenge regarding the cause preventing loss. If it is the cause preventing phenomena from being lost, then since wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena would all equally possess this attainment, these mutually incompatible states should manifest all at once. Second, the conclusion. Therefore neither position is tenable.

items.title: Section: Mastery as a Second Sense of "Attainment" — and Three Kinds of Accomplishment Begin

items.zh: 又生因者，所謂各別緣所攝受諸法自種。不離散因者，謂由餘緣現在前故，餘緣離散。若於引發緣中，勢力自在，假立為得。以此自在為依止故，所有士夫補特伽羅。雖彼彼法已起、已滅，若欲希彼復現在前，便能速疾引發諸緣，令得生起，是故亦說此名為得。當知此得略有三種。一、種子成就，二、自在成就，三、現行成就。若所有染污法、諸無記法、生得善法，不由功用而現行者，彼諸種子若未為奢摩他之所損伏，若未為聖道之所永害，若不為邪見損伏諸善如斷善根者，如是名為種子成就。
items.en:
Third, the explanation; first, the generating cause. The generating cause is simply each phenomenon's own seed, taken hold of by its own distinct condition. Second, the cause of dispersal. The cause of dispersal is simply that when some other condition becomes present, yet other conditions correspondingly disperse.
Second, according to mastery over a condition; first, stating this provisional designation. When one's mastery over an inducing condition is forceful, this is provisionally called attainment. Second, explaining this mastery. Relying on this mastery, a person, even when this or that phenomenon has already arisen and ceased, if they wish for it to manifest again, can swiftly induce the conditions and bring about its arising — for this reason, this too is called attainment.
Second, broadly explaining the three kinds; first, stating and listing. One should know that attainment is, in brief, of three kinds: seed-accomplishment, mastery-accomplishment, and manifest-activity-accomplishment.
Second, explaining each; first, seed-accomplishment; first, stating it. Whenever any defiled phenomenon, neutral phenomenon, or innate wholesome quality manifesting without special effort has its seed neither suppressed by the power of calming meditation, nor permanently destroyed by the noble path, nor undermined by wrong view as in severing one's own wholesome roots, this is called seed-accomplishment.

items.zh: 所以者何？乃至此種子未被損伏、未被永害，爾時彼染污等法，若

items.title: Section: Manifest-Activity Completes the Three Accomplishments — And "Attainment" Is Fully Resolved into Provisional Designation

items.zh: 現行、若不現行，皆說名成就故。若加行所生善法及一分無記法，生緣所攝受增盛因種子，名自在成就。若現在諸法自相現前轉，名現行成就。復次，云何命根？
items.en:
Third, manifest-activity-accomplishment. When a present phenomenon's own characteristic is currently manifesting and functioning, this is called manifest-activity-accomplishment.
Second, the life faculty; first, the question posed. Furthermore, what is the life faculty?

items.title: Section: What the Life Faculty Really Is — Lifespan, Warmth, and Consciousness Combined, and Three Ways Life Can End

items.zh: 謂由先業，於彼彼處所生自體所有住時限量勢分，說名為壽、生氣、命根。此復多種差別。謂定、不定、隨轉、不隨轉，若少、若多，若有邊際、若無邊際，若自勢力轉、若非自勢力轉。
items.en:
Second, the explanation; first, stating its establishment. Due to past karma, the span, limit, quantity, force, and duration by which one's own resultant embodiment, arisen in this or that place, continues to abide — this is called lifespan, vital energy, and the life faculty.
Second, explaining its distinctions; first, stating and listing. This is further of many kinds: fixed or unfixed, following its course or not following it, short or long, bounded or unbounded, and determined by one's own controlling power or not so determined.

blocks.text: Three people meet impermanence: the householder grieves, the ascetic suppresses, the noble disciple is freed. Then the treatise examines "attainment" and "life" themselves.
Beings rely on nourishment until their lifespan is exhausted; the external world abides for a great eon. Master Cháng Bǎi: beings sustain life on four foods (Day 454).
Feelings and states abide as long as their condition is present. Master Cháng Bǎi: different conditions bring different feelings.
Master Cháng Bǎi: what has arisen ceases of itself, immediately; ceasing does not await a cause. Separation is when the thing itself is not broken, but outer conditions part us from it.

Householders reflect on only three kinds of impermanence, grieve, and cannot develop revulsion; outsiders reach partial revulsion; noble disciples reach it completely. Master Cháng Bǎi: without right view, even absorption is only a stone pressing on grass.

A cause taken up and strengthened by a condition is called attainment; it is a provisional name. Master Cháng Bǎi: Yogācāra's theory of seeds explains karma and result without a real thing called "attainment".
By seed, by mastery, by manifest activity. Master Cháng Bǎi: one who has "severed wholesome roots" has cut off only their manifestation, not the seed of good.

"The span and force of duration of the embodiment arisen through past karma." Master Cháng Bǎi: lifespan, warmth, and consciousness together are the life faculty; only when all three are gone is life gone, and the most important is the store-consciousness.
Even someone who has "severed wholesome roots" keeps the seed of good. The consequence is hopeful: no one is beyond hope.

quiz.q: What are the inner and outer sides of "continuity abiding"?
options: beings rely on absorption and abide until life ends; the external world arises and ceases each moment, not lasting an eon
beings on the four foods abide for a great eon; the world abides until they die
beings rely on the four foods and abide until life ends; the external world abides for a great eon
beings rely on norms until life ends; the world abides forever through karma
quiz.why: The treatise describes beings relying on nourishment until their lifespan is exhausted, and the external world abiding for a great eon. Master Cháng Bǎi: beings sustain life on four kinds of food, solid food, contact, volition, and consciousness, until life ends; the external world abiding for a great eon is its continuity abiding.

quiz.q: The English has "continuity of the perceived object" for 緣相續住. Is 緣 here the perceived object?
options: yes, the object: so long as an object is before one, feeling does not change
it is karmic affinity: bonds between beings decide how long things continue
not the object: it is that distinct conditions are present and feelings and other phenomena abide with them; the English narrows it
it is clinging: the mind holding an object undistracted is undistracted abiding
quiz.why: The treatise says feelings and wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral phenomena abide for as long as their distinct condition is present. Master Cháng Bǎi: different conditions bring different feelings and mental states. So 緣 means conditions in general, as the English sentence itself says ("condition"), yet its label narrows this to "the perceived object."

quiz.q: The English has "having arisen, soon cease" for 生已尋滅. Compared with the lecture, how should 尋 be understood?
options: ceasing before long: phenomena must first last for some time and only then are destroyed
seeking: phenomena seek their own ending
afterwards: they cease once an outer condition arrives
ceasing right upon arising: phenomena arise and cease each moment, not after a while
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi explains impermanence of destruction as conditioned phenomena arising and ceasing each moment, and adds that what has arisen ceases of itself. So 尋 means immediately. The English "soon cease" may suggest an interval between arising and ceasing, which neither the treatise nor the lecture intends here.

quiz.q: What does Master Cháng Bǎi say is the consciousness-only view of ceasing?
options: phenomena, once arisen, must await an outer condition to cease
phenomena cease of themselves once arisen; ceasing does not await a cause
arising awaits a cause, and ceasing is the work of a real mark of ceasing
the ceasing of phenomena is determined by karma
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: consciousness-only teaches that phenomena cease of themselves once arisen; having arisen they naturally cease, and ceasing does not await a cause. It needs no conditions and perishes by itself, which is called impermanence of destruction.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi distinguish impermanence of change from impermanence of dispersal?
options: in change the thing itself goes from good to bad; in dispersal it is unspoiled but separated by outer conditions
in change the thing is unspoiled and only separated by outer conditions; in dispersal it goes from good to bad itself
change lies in the future; dispersal lies in the present
change is existing after absence; dispersal is ceasing after arising
quiz.why: The treatise speaks of desirable possessions, unchanged in themselves, being scattered. Master Cháng Bǎi: the thing itself is not broken, but outer conditions have separated them, whereas impermanence of change means conditioned things that were good have turned bad.

quiz.q: How do heedless householders respond to impermanence?
options: they reflect much and develop some revulsion, but only in part
they reflect fully and reach complete revulsion and liberation
they do not reflect on impermanence at all and feel no grief
they reflect only on change, dispersal, and present falling away, grieve, and yet cannot develop revulsion
quiz.why: The treatise distinguishes three responses. Householders reflect on only three kinds of impermanence, grieve, and cannot develop revulsion; outsiders reach partial revulsion; noble disciples reach it completely. Master Cháng Bǎi: though impermanence is so painful for them, they still do not wish to leave the world behind.

quiz.q: Why, according to Master Cháng Bǎi, can outsiders develop revulsion only in part?
options: they have no absorption, so their freedom from desire is incomplete
they reflect only on present falling away, not the other kinds
they reject cause and effect and so cannot leave desire at all
lacking right view, even absorption is a stone pressing on grass; they suppress afflictions but cannot sever them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: for lack of right view, even attaining absorption is only a stone pressing on grass and does not finally remove desire; outsiders can at most suppress afflictions and cannot wholly sever them. The treatise says they do reflect much on impermanence and reach some revulsion, so the problem is not lack of absorption.

quiz.q: Does the treatise regard attainment as substantially real or as provisional?
options: substantially real: it is the generating cause of conditioned phenomena
substantially real: it is the cause keeping phenomena from being lost
provisional: a cause taken hold of and strengthened by a condition is called attainment
unconditioned: neither arising nor ceasing, outside conditioned phenomena
quiz.why: The treatise says a cause taken hold of and strengthened by a condition is called attainment, and by this reasoning attainment is provisional. Master Cháng Bǎi: Mahāyāna consciousness-only establishes seeds, which readily explains karma and result, and holds attainment and the like to be provisionally established.

quiz.q: Into which three accomplishments does the treatise divide attainment?
options: seed-accomplishment, effort-accomplishment, and ripened-result-accomplishment
accomplishment by hearing, by reflection, and by cultivation
past, future, and present accomplishment
seed-accomplishment, mastery-accomplishment, and manifest-activity-accomplishment
quiz.why: The treatise lists seed-accomplishment, mastery-accomplishment, and manifest-activity-accomplishment. Master Cháng Bǎi explains the last: when conditioned phenomena are presently active, this is called manifest-activity-accomplishment.

quiz.q: What exactly does a person who has "severed wholesome roots" sever, according to Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: the manifesting of good, not the seed of good
the seed of good, so that good can never arise again
the seeds of good and evil alike, becoming neutral
the seeds of defilement, as the noble path destroys them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: severing wholesome roots means that this person has no wholesome mental factors manifesting, only evil phenomena; the wholesome roots are cut off, yet it is not the seed of good that is cut, only its manifestation.

quiz.q: How does the treatise define the life faculty?
options: the time a body survives, produced by present nourishment
by past karma, the span and force of duration of the resultant embodiment, called lifespan, vital energy, and the life faculty
the unbroken flow of in-breath and out-breath
a real life-substance existing apart from form and mind
quiz.why: The treatise defines the life faculty as the span and force of duration of the embodiment arisen through past karma. Master Cháng Bǎi: lifespan, warmth, and consciousness together are called the life faculty; a living person has all three.

quiz.q: Among lifespan, warmth, and consciousness, what does Master Cháng Bǎi say is most important?
options: warmth
lifespan
the store-consciousness
the sixth, mental consciousness
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: only when lifespan, warmth, and consciousness are all completely gone is the life faculty gone, and among them the most important is the store-consciousness.
